subject: Biology
title: Morphology of Flowering Plants
summary: The external form of a flowering plant, organ by organ, in NCERT order: the root and its regions, the stem, the leaf (venation, simple and compound leaves, phyllotaxy), the inflorescence, the flower with all four whorls, aestivation and placentation, the fruit, the dicot and monocot seed, and finally how to write a semi-technical description with a floral formula and floral diagram, using the family Solanaceae. It is a vocabulary-and-diagram chapter: the marks go to the student who uses the exact NCERT term, quotes the NCERT example and draws a clean labelled figure, and the same terms return in Class 12 (Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants) and in NEET every year.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school, so there is no fixed board weightage. This chapter sits in Unit II, Structural Organisation in Plants and Animals, which the CBSE syllabus allots 11 marks shared with Anatomy of Flowering Plants and Structural Organisation in Animals. In a typical school final this chapter alone brings 5 to 7 marks: one or two 1-mark items (an MCQ, an Assertion–Reason or a fill-in), a 2-mark definition or distinction, a 3-mark question on aestivation, placentation or modifications, and quite often a 5-mark question on the parts of a flower, placentation with diagrams, or the semi-technical description of Solanaceae. In NEET it is one of the heaviest scoring chapters of Class 11 botany, with two to four questions almost every year lifted straight from NCERT lines and examples.

question_types.note: Match a modification to its example (prop root of banyan, stilt root of maize, pneumatophore of Rhizophora, tendril of cucumber, thorn of Citrus, spine of Opuntia, phyllode of Australian Acacia); identify the placentation of pea, mustard, Dianthus, sunflower; the aestivation of Calotropis, china rose, Cassia, pea; the phyllotaxy of Alstonia, Calotropis, mustard; hypogynous, perigynous or epigynous examples; the ploidy or role of aleurone layer, scutellum, coleoptile; the floral formula symbols; Solanaceae characters.

Flower is a modified shoot; potato is a stem and sweet potato a root; bud in the axil of a petiole but not of a leaflet; cymose flowers open in basipetal order; parthenocarpic fruits are seedless; mango is a drupe; monocot seeds are generally endospermic; epigynous flower has an inferior ovary.

Define venation and name its two types with examples; distinguish prop roots from stilt roots, tap root from fibrous root, racemose from cymose, apocarpous from syncarpous, simple from compound leaf; give the function of root hairs, pneumatophores, aleurone layer, coleoptile; write the floral formula of Solanaceae; justify that onion bulb or potato tuber is a stem; name the four regions of a root.

Describe the four types of aestivation with one example each; describe placentation types with labelled sketches; explain the three positions of the ovary on the thalamus (hypogynous, perigynous, epigynous); explain phyllotaxy with examples; describe modifications of root, stem or leaf for a given function; label a maize grain or gram seed and give the function of the endosperm; distinguish pinnately from palmately compound leaves; explain the four whorls of a flower briefly.

Describe the parts of a typical angiosperm flower with a labelled diagram; describe the various types of placentation with diagrams; write the semi-technical description, floral formula and floral diagram of Solanaceae (Solanum nigrum) with its economic importance; describe the modifications of stem for storage, support, protection and vegetative propagation; describe the structure of a dicot and a monocot seed with labelled diagrams.

A passage on potato, ginger and sweet potato asking the student to tell stem from root by nodes, buds and scale leaves; a passage comparing a soaked gram seed with a maize grain; a floral formula given and the student asked to name the family, symmetry, ovary position and placentation; a description of a mangrove plant and its roots.

sections.heading: Introduction: the body of a flowering plant
sections.body:
Morphology is the study of external form and structure. The previous chapters classified plants; this chapter looks at what a typical flowering plant (an angiosperm) actually looks like from the outside, organ by organ, so that you can describe any plant you are handed in the language a botanist uses. Every term in this chapter is one the examiner expects verbatim, so learn the NCERT word and the NCERT example together.

The body of a flowering plant is one axis with two ends. The part below the soil is the root system, which develops from the radicle of the embryo. The part above the soil is the shoot system, which develops from the plumule. The shoot carries the stem, the leaves at its nodes, the flowers, and after fertilisation the fruits and seeds. NCERT Figure 5.1 shows all of these on a single plant, with a leaf at each node, an axillary bud in the angle between the leaf and the stem, and a flower at the tip. A very common 1-mark item asks you to identify one of these parts or to state which embryonic structure a root or a shoot develops from.

Roots, stems and leaves are the vegetative organs; the flower, fruit and seed are the reproductive organs. Yet plants do not always keep to their basic plan. A part is sometimes changed in form and function to do a different job, and this is called a modification. Underground potato is a stem, aerial prop roots of banyan are roots, the spines of Opuntia are leaves. Telling a modified part from what it looks like at first glance is the skill the whole chapter builds, and the rule is always the same: judge an organ by its external features (nodes, internodes, buds, scale leaves, root cap, root hairs), not by where it sits.

A note on the syllabus: the rationalised NCERT print keeps the root, stem, leaf, inflorescence, flower, fruit, seed, semi-technical description and the family Solanaceae. The sub-sections on modifications of root, stem and leaf and the families Fabaceae and Liliaceae were trimmed from the print, but modifications are still asked in almost every school paper and in NEET, so this guide covers them fully and marks them as extension sections.
sections.tip: Root from radicle, shoot from plumule. Write it as the first line whenever a question asks about the origin of the root or shoot system.

sections.heading: 5.1 The Root: types and regions
sections.body:
In most dicotyledonous plants the radicle elongates directly into the primary root, which grows into the soil and bears lateral roots of several orders (secondary, tertiary and so on). The primary root together with its branches is the tap root system, as in mustard. In monocotyledons the primary root is short-lived and is replaced by a large number of roots arising from the base of the stem; this is the fibrous root system, as in wheat. In some plants roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle; these are adventitious roots, as in grass, Monstera and the banyan tree. Note the exam distinction: a fibrous root system is a whole system of thin roots in monocots, whereas adventitious root is any root that does not come from the radicle, whether it forms a system or not.

The main functions of the root system are absorption of water and minerals from the soil, providing proper anchorage to the plant parts, storing reserve food material and synthesis of plant growth regulators. Give all four when asked for functions.

Regions of the root (5.1.1). From the tip upward there are four regions. (1) The root cap: a thimble-like structure covering the apex, protecting the tender tip as it pushes through the soil. (2) The region of meristematic activity, a few millimetres above the cap: its cells are very small, thin-walled and with dense protoplasm, and they divide repeatedly. (3) The region of elongation: cells proximal to the meristem undergo rapid elongation and enlargement and are responsible for the growth of the root in length. (4) The region of maturation: the cells of the elongation zone gradually differentiate and mature. From this region some epidermal cells form very fine and delicate thread-like structures called root hairs, which absorb water and minerals from the soil. Root hairs are unicellular extensions of epidermal cells; they are short-lived and are replaced as the root grows.

The examiner likes a labelled sketch of the root tip (NCERT Figure 5.3) with these four regions and root hairs marked, and a one-line function for each region.
sections.tip: The region of elongation is where growth in length happens; the meristematic region only supplies the new cells. Students swap the two.

sections.heading: 5.1.2 Modifications of Root (extension, still asked)
sections.body:
Roots in some plants change their shape and structure and become modified to perform functions other than absorption and conduction of water and minerals. They are modified for support, storage of food and respiration. Learn each with its NCERT example; the examples are what score.

For storage. Tap roots of carrot and turnip and adventitious roots of sweet potato get swollen and store food. So carrot, turnip and radish are swollen tap roots, and sweet potato is a swollen adventitious root. This is the trap behind the classic question 'potato is a stem, sweet potato is a root': sweet potato has no nodes, no buds and no scale leaves, and it bears lateral rootlets.

For support. Hanging structures that support a banyan tree are called prop roots; they grow down from horizontal branches, enter the soil and act like pillars. The stems of maize and sugarcane have supporting roots coming out of the lower nodes of the stem; these are called stilt roots. The distinction the examiner wants: prop roots arise from the branches high up and are thick and pillar-like; stilt roots arise from the lower nodes of the stem, in a cluster, and grow obliquely into the soil.

For respiration. In some plants that grow in swampy areas, many roots come out of the ground and grow vertically upwards. Such roots are called pneumatophores, and they help to get oxygen for respiration, as in Rhizophora growing in mangrove swamps. The soil there is waterlogged and poor in oxygen, so the roots turn upward and take in air through small pores.

A 3-mark question often names three plants (say banyan, turnip, Rhizophora) and asks you to name the modification and its function. Answer in three clear lines: plant, name of modification, function.
sections.tip: Carrot, turnip, radish: tap root. Sweet potato: adventitious root. Potato: stem. Do not let the word 'potato' fool you.

sections.heading: 5.2 The Stem
sections.body:
The stem is the ascending part of the axis bearing branches, leaves, flowers and fruits. It develops from the plumule of the embryo of a germinating seed. The stem bears nodes and internodes: the region of the stem where leaves are born is the node, and the portion between two nodes is the internode. The stem bears buds, which may be terminal (at the tip) or axillary (in the angle between leaf and stem). The stem is generally green when young and later often becomes woody and dark brown.

The main function of the stem is spreading out branches bearing leaves, flowers and fruits. It conducts water, minerals and photosynthates. Some stems perform the function of storage of food, support, protection and vegetative propagation. That list of functions is the full 2-mark answer.

What makes a stem a stem is the presence of nodes and internodes, buds (terminal and axillary) and leaves or scale leaves. This is the test you apply to any doubtful underground part. Potato has nodes with 'eyes' (each eye is a group of axillary buds in the axil of a scale leaf), ginger has nodes, internodes and scaly leaves, onion bulb has a short conical stem carrying fleshy leaves and a terminal bud. None of them has a root cap or root hairs. So all three are stems. Hence the NCERT exercise statement 'underground parts of a plant are not always roots'.

Herbaceous stems are soft and green, woody stems are hard and brown. Stems may be erect, or weak and creeping (trailing) or climbing with the help of tendrils or hooks. Remember these plain descriptors; they are the words you will use in the vegetative part of a semi-technical description: stem herbaceous or woody, aerial, erect, cylindrical, branched, solid or hollow, hairy or glabrous.
sections.tip: A bud is the surest sign of a stem. If a question asks how you know potato is a stem, say: it has nodes and internodes, and its eyes are axillary buds in the axils of scale leaves.

sections.heading: 5.2.1 Modifications of Stem (extension, still asked)
sections.body:
The stem may not always be typically like what it is expected to be. It is modified to perform different functions. Group the modifications by function, as NCERT does, and attach an example to each.

Underground stems for storage and perennation. Underground stems of potato, ginger, turmeric, zaminkand and Colocasia are modified to store food in them. They also act as organs of perennation to tide over conditions unfavourable for growth. Potato is a tuber (a swollen tip of an underground branch with eyes), ginger and turmeric are rhizomes (horizontal, with nodes, internodes and scaly leaves), zaminkand and Colocasia are corms (short, vertical, swollen, with a terminal bud).

Tendrils for climbing. Stem tendrils which develop from axillary buds are slender and spirally coiled and help plants to climb, as in gourds (cucumber, pumpkins, watermelon) and grapevines.

Thorns for protection. Axillary buds of stems may also get modified into woody, straight and pointed thorns, as in Citrus and Bougainvillea. They protect plants from browsing animals.

Photosynthesis in arid regions. Some plants of arid regions modify their stems into flattened (Opuntia) or fleshy cylindrical (Euphorbia) structures. They contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis; such a stem is called a phylloclade.

Vegetative propagation. Underground stems of some plants such as grass and strawberry spread to new niches and, when older parts die, new plants are formed (runner). In plants like mint and jasmine a slender lateral branch arises from the base of the main axis and, after growing aerially for some time, arches downwards to touch the ground (stolon). A lateral branch with short internodes and each node bearing a rosette of leaves and a tuft of roots is found in aquatic plants like Pistia and Eichhornia (offset). In banana, pineapple and Chrysanthemum the lateral branches originate from the basal and underground portion of the main stem, grow horizontally beneath the soil and then come out obliquely upward, giving rise to leafy shoots (sucker).

Also know the pair that is asked in 'differentiate' questions: a phylloclade is a green flattened or fleshy stem (Opuntia), whereas a phyllode is a green flattened petiole doing the work of the leaf (Australian Acacia).
sections.tip: Tendrils of cucumber are stem tendrils from axillary buds; tendrils of pea are leaf tendrils from leaflets. The examiner sets exactly this contrast.

sections.heading: 5.3 The Leaf: parts, venation, types and phyllotaxy
sections.body:
The leaf is a lateral, generally flattened structure borne on the stem. It develops at the node and bears a bud in its axil. The axillary bud later develops into a branch. Leaves originate from shoot apical meristems and are arranged in an acropetal order (oldest at the base, youngest at the tip). They are the most important vegetative organs for photosynthesis.

A typical leaf has three main parts: leaf base, petiole and lamina. The leaf is attached to the stem by the leaf base and may bear two lateral small leaf-like structures called stipules. In monocotyledons the leaf base expands into a sheath covering the stem partially or wholly. In some leguminous plants the leaf base may become swollen, which is called the pulvinus. The petiole helps hold the blade to light; long thin flexible petioles allow leaf blades to flutter in wind, thereby cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to the leaf surface. The lamina or leaf blade is the green expanded part with veins and veinlets. There is usually a middle prominent vein, the midrib. Veins provide rigidity to the leaf blade and act as channels of transport for water, minerals and food materials.

5.3.1 Venation. The arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina of a leaf is termed venation. When the veinlets form a network, the venation is reticulate (dicotyledons). When the veins run parallel to each other within a lamina, the venation is parallel (monocotyledons). This is a favourite 2-mark question and a favourite MCQ.

5.3.2 Types of leaves. A leaf is simple when its lamina is entire or when incised, the incisions do not touch the midrib. When the incisions of the lamina reach up to the midrib breaking it into a number of leaflets, the leaf is called compound. A bud is present in the axil of the petiole in both simple and compound leaves, but not in the axil of leaflets of the compound leaf; this is how you tell a leaflet from a leaf. Compound leaves are of two types. In a pinnately compound leaf a number of leaflets are present on a common axis, the rachis, which represents the midrib of the leaf, as in neem. In a palmately compound leaf the leaflets are attached at a common point, at the tip of the petiole, as in silk cotton (Bombax).

5.3.3 Phyllotaxy. Phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch. It is of three types. In alternate phyllotaxy a single leaf arises at each node in alternate manner, as in china rose, mustard and sunflower. In opposite phyllotaxy a pair of leaves arises at each node and lies opposite to each other, as in Calotropis and guava. If more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl, it is whorled, as in Alstonia.
sections.tip: Neem is pinnately compound, silk cotton is palmately compound. When drawing, show the rachis clearly in neem and the single attachment point in silk cotton, and mark the axillary bud at the base of the petiole, not on the leaflets.

sections.heading: 5.3.4 Modifications of Leaves (extension, still asked)
sections.body:
Leaves are often modified to perform functions other than photosynthesis. Five modifications appear in NCERT, each with one example, and a 3-mark question ('How do various leaf modifications help plants?') expects all five.

Tendrils. Leaves are converted into tendrils for climbing, as in peas. In pea the terminal leaflets of the pinnately compound leaf become thread-like, coiling tendrils that hold the plant up on a support. Contrast with the stem tendrils of cucumber and grapevine.

Spines. Leaves are converted into spines for defence, as in cacti. Reducing the leaf to a spine also cuts water loss in a desert plant; photosynthesis is taken over by the green flattened stem, the phylloclade (Opuntia).

Fleshy leaves for storage. The fleshy leaves of onion and garlic store food. The onion bulb is a short conical stem carrying these fleshy leaves; the outer dry scales are also leaves.

Phyllode. In some plants such as Australian Acacia the leaves are small and short-lived. The petioles in these plants expand, become green and synthesise food. This flattened green petiole is a phyllode. (Phyllode = petiole; phylloclade = stem.)

Insect-catching leaves. Leaves of certain insectivorous plants such as pitcher plant (Nepenthes) and venus fly trap (Dionaea) are modified to trap insects. In the pitcher plant the lamina forms the pitcher, the apex of the leaf the lid, and the petiole a tendril-like stalk; the plant grows in nitrogen-poor soil and digests the insect for nitrogen.

When answering, always pair the modification with its function and its example: 'Leaf tendril, for climbing, pea.' Three words score; a paragraph without the example does not.
sections.tip: Spines of Opuntia are leaves, but the thorns of Citrus and Bougainvillea are stems (modified axillary buds). Spine = leaf, thorn = stem, in NCERT usage.

sections.heading: 5.4 The Inflorescence
sections.body:
A flower is a modified shoot. The shoot apical meristem changes to a floral meristem. Internodes do not elongate, so the axis gets condensed. The apex produces different kinds of floral appendages laterally at successive nodes instead of leaves. When a shoot tip transforms into a flower, it is always solitary. This four-line argument is the complete answer to the NCERT exercise 'Justify: flower is a modified shoot', and the examiner ticks each line.

The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is termed the inflorescence. Depending on whether the apex gets converted into a flower or continues to grow, two major types are defined.

Racemose inflorescence. The main axis continues to grow (it has unlimited growth), and the flowers are borne laterally in an acropetal succession: the oldest flowers are at the base and the youngest near the tip. The main axis never ends in a flower. Examples usually quoted: mustard, radish, Fabaceae plants.

Cymose inflorescence. The main axis terminates in a flower, hence it is of limited growth. The flowers are borne in a basipetal order: the terminal flower is the oldest and the younger flowers arise below it on lateral branches. Examples: Solanum (as NCERT notes under Solanaceae), jasmine, Calotropis.

Two differences are enough for a 2-mark question: (i) growth of main axis, unlimited versus limited; (ii) order of flowers, acropetal versus basipetal. A third if asked: the main axis does not end in a flower versus ends in a flower.

Note the phrase 'basis for the different types of inflorescence' in NCERT exercise 13: the basis is whether the apex is converted into a flower or continues to grow. Say that first, then describe the two types.
sections.tip: Acropetal: oldest at base, youngest at tip (racemose). Basipetal: oldest at the top, youngest at the base (cymose). Tie each word to its inflorescence and you will not confuse them.

sections.heading: 5.5 The Flower: symmetry, merosity and position of the ovary
sections.body:
The flower is the reproductive unit in the angiosperms. It is meant for sexual reproduction. A typical flower has four different kinds of whorls arranged successively on the swollen end of the stalk or pedicel, called the thalamus or receptacle. These are calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium. Calyx and corolla are accessory organs, while androecium and gynoecium are reproductive organs. In some flowers like lily the calyx and corolla are not distinct and are termed perianth. When a flower has both androecium and gynoecium it is bisexual; a flower having either only stamens or only carpels is unisexual.

Symmetry. In symmetry, the flower may be actinomorphic or zygomorphic. When a flower can be divided into two equal radial halves in any radial plane passing through the centre, it is actinomorphic (radial symmetry), as in mustard, datura, chilli. When it can be divided into two similar halves only in one particular vertical plane, it is zygomorphic (bilateral symmetry), as in pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia. A flower is asymmetric (irregular) if it cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane passing through the centre, as in canna.

Merosity. A flower may be trimerous, tetramerous or pentamerous when the floral appendages are in multiples of 3, 4 or 5 respectively. Monocots are typically trimerous (lily), mustard is tetramerous, Solanaceae and Fabaceae are pentamerous.

Bracts. Flowers with bracts, reduced leaves found at the base of the pedicel, are called bracteate, and those without bracts ebracteate.

Position of the ovary on the thalamus. Based on the position of calyx, corolla and androecium in respect of the ovary, flowers are of three kinds. In hypogynous flowers the gynoecium occupies the highest position while the other parts are situated below it; the ovary is said to be superior, as in mustard, china rose and brinjal. In perigynous flowers the gynoecium is situated in the centre and the other parts of the flower are located on the rim of the thalamus almost at the same level; the ovary is said to be half inferior, as in plum, rose, peach. In epigynous flowers the margin of the thalamus grows upward enclosing the ovary completely and getting fused with it, and the other parts of the flower arise above the ovary; the ovary is said to be inferior, as in guava, cucumber and the ray florets of sunflower. NCERT exercise 15 asks exactly this, and a 3-mark answer needs the three definitions, the three ovary positions and the examples, with three small sketches (NCERT figure).
sections.tip: Hypogynous: superior ovary. Perigynous: half inferior. Epigynous: inferior. Draw the thalamus as a cup in perigynous and as a cup fused with the ovary in epigynous.

sections.heading: 5.5.1 Parts of a flower: calyx, corolla and aestivation
sections.body:
Each flower normally has four floral whorls: calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium, from outside inward. Learn the terms for each whorl exactly.

Calyx. The calyx is the outermost whorl and its members are called sepals. Generally sepals are green, leaf-like and protect the flower in the bud stage. The calyx may be gamosepalous (sepals united) or polysepalous (sepals free). In Solanaceae the calyx is gamosepalous and also persistent, remaining attached to the fruit (look at the green cap on a brinjal or tomato).

Corolla. The corolla is composed of petals. Petals are usually brightly coloured to attract insects for pollination. Like the calyx, the corolla may be gamopetalous (petals united) or polypetalous (petals free). The shape and colour of the corolla vary greatly; it may be tubular, bell-shaped, funnel-shaped or wheel-shaped.

Aestivation. The mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in a floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl is known as aestivation. The main types are valvate, twisted, imbricate and vexillary. When sepals or petals in a whorl just touch one another at the margin without overlapping, it is valvate, as in Calotropis. If one margin of the appendage overlaps that of the next one and so on, it is twisted, as in china rose, lady's finger and cotton. If the margins of sepals or petals overlap one another but not in any particular direction, it is imbricate, as in Cassia and gulmohur. In pea and bean flowers there are five petals, the largest (standard) overlaps the two lateral petals (wings), which in turn overlap the two smallest anterior petals (keel); this is vexillary or papilionaceous aestivation, as in pea and bean.

The 3-mark version of this question gives the four names and asks for the definition, an example and a small top-view sketch of each (the NCERT figure: five petals drawn as a ring, edges touching in valvate, each overlapping the next in one direction in twisted, overlapping without pattern in imbricate, and the standard-wings-keel arrangement in vexillary). Draw the sketches; they are the difference between 2 and 3 marks.
sections.tip: Aestivation is about the bud, and about members of the same whorl. Twisted is 'one direction', imbricate is 'no particular direction'; that single phrase separates the two in the marking scheme.

sections.heading: 5.5.1 Parts of a flower: androecium, gynoecium and placentation
sections.body:
Androecium. The androecium is composed of stamens. Each stamen, which represents the male reproductive organ, consists of a stalk or filament and an anther. Each anther is usually bilobed, and each lobe has two chambers, the pollen sacs. Pollen grains are produced in pollen sacs. A sterile stamen is called a staminode. Stamens of a flower may be united with other members such as petals or among themselves. When stamens are attached to the petals they are epipetalous, as in brinjal; when attached to the perianth they are epiphyllous, as in lily. The stamens in a flower may either remain free (polyandrous) or may be united in varying degrees: in one bunch or one bundle, monadelphous (china rose); in two bundles, diadelphous (pea); in more than two bundles, polyadelphous (citrus). There may be variation in the length of filaments within a flower, as in Salvia and mustard.

Gynoecium. The gynoecium is the female reproductive part of the flower and is made up of one or more carpels. A carpel consists of three parts, the stigma, style and ovary. The ovary is the enlarged basal part, on which lies the elongated tube, the style. The style connects the ovary to the stigma. The stigma is usually at the tip of the style and is the receptive surface for pollen grains. Each ovary bears one or more ovules attached to a flattened cushion-like placenta. When more than one carpel is present, they may be free, as in lotus and rose, and are called apocarpous; they are termed syncarpous when carpels are fused, as in mustard and tomato. After fertilisation the ovules develop into seeds and the ovary matures into a fruit.

Placentation. The arrangement of ovules within the ovary is known as placentation. It is of five types. Marginal: the placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary and the ovules are borne on this ridge forming two rows, as in pea. Axile: the placenta is axial and the ovules are attached to it in a multilocular ovary, as in china rose, tomato and lemon. Parietal: the ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or on the peripheral part; the ovary is one-chambered but becomes two-chambered due to the formation of a false septum, as in mustard and Argemone. Free central: the ovules are borne on the central axis and septa are absent, as in Dianthus and Primrose. Basal: the placenta develops at the base of the ovary and a single ovule is attached to it, as in sunflower and marigold.

The 5-mark placentation question needs the definition, the five types each with a one-line description and example, and five transverse-section sketches (NCERT figure). Draw a circle for the ovary wall and place the ovules where the placenta is: at the suture (marginal), on the central axis with septa (axile), on the wall (parietal), on a central column without septa (free central), one ovule at the bottom in a longitudinal view (basal).
sections.tip: Axile and free central both have ovules on a central column; the difference is the septa. Axile has septa (chambers), free central has none. Write that sentence and you have separated them.

sections.heading: 5.6 The Fruit
sections.body:
The fruit is a characteristic feature of the flowering plants. It is a mature or ripened ovary, developed after fertilisation. If a fruit is formed without fertilisation of the ovary, it is called a parthenocarpic fruit; such fruits are seedless, as in banana and some grapes.

Generally the fruit consists of a wall or pericarp and seeds. The pericarp may be dry or fleshy. When the pericarp is thick and fleshy it is differentiated into three layers: the outer epicarp, the middle mesocarp and the inner endocarp.

NCERT uses two fruits to show this. In mango and coconut the fruit is known as a drupe. They develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one-seeded. In mango the pericarp is well differentiated into an outer thin epicarp (the skin), a middle fleshy edible mesocarp (the pulp) and an inner stony hard endocarp (the 'stone' around the seed). In coconut the mesocarp is fibrous (the coir), the endocarp is the hard shell and the edible part is the endosperm of the seed, not the pericarp. 'Which part of mango is edible?' is a routine 1-mark question; the answer is mesocarp.

Two more terms are asked in school papers though they sit outside the NCERT text. A true fruit develops from the ovary alone (mango, tomato). A false fruit (pseudocarp) develops from the ovary together with other floral parts such as the thalamus, as in apple and cashew, where the fleshy edible part is the thalamus. Keep the answer to that level; the examiner wants the source of the fleshy part, not a classification of fruit types.
sections.tip: Drupe = mango and coconut, monocarpellary, superior ovary, one seed, stony endocarp. Give all five points if the question carries 2 marks.

sections.heading: 5.7 The Seed: dicot and monocot
sections.body:
The ovules after fertilisation develop into seeds. A seed is made up of a seed coat and an embryo. The embryo is made up of a radicle, an embryonal axis and one (as in wheat, maize) or two cotyledons (as in gram and pea).

5.7.1 Structure of a dicotyledonous seed (gram, bean). The outermost covering is the seed coat, which has two layers, the outer testa and the inner tegmen. The hilum is a scar on the seed coat through which the developing seed was attached to the fruit. Above the hilum is a small pore, the micropyle, through which water enters at germination. Within the seed coat is the embryo, consisting of an embryonal axis and two cotyledons. The cotyledons are often fleshy and full of reserve food materials. At the two ends of the embryonal axis are present the radicle and the plumule. In some seeds such as castor the endosperm, formed as a result of double fertilisation, is a food-storing tissue; such seeds are endospermic. In plants such as bean, gram and pea the endosperm is not present in mature seeds because it is consumed by the developing embryo; they are non-endospermic.

5.7.2 Structure of a monocotyledonous seed (maize). Generally monocotyledonous seeds are endospermic, but some, as in orchids, are non-endospermic. In the cereals such as maize the seed coat is membranous and generally fused with the fruit wall (which is why a maize grain is technically a fruit, a caryopsis). The endosperm is bulky and stores food. The outer covering of the endosperm separates the embryo by a proteinous layer called the aleurone layer. The embryo is small and situated in a groove at one end of the endosperm. It consists of one large and shield-shaped cotyledon known as the scutellum and a short axis with a plumule and a radicle. The plumule and radicle are enclosed in sheaths called the coleoptile and coleorhiza respectively.

NCERT exercise 7 asks for labelled diagrams of a gram seed and a vertical section of a maize grain, and this is the most reliable diagram question of the chapter. The maize V.S. must show: seed coat fused with the fruit wall, endosperm, aleurone layer, scutellum, coleoptile, plumule, radicle, coleorhiza. The gram seed must show: testa, tegmen (as seed coat), hilum, micropyle, cotyledons, plumule, radicle. Practise both until each takes under two minutes.
sections.tip: Coleoptile covers the plumule, coleorhiza covers the radicle. The names carry their own clue: -rhiza means root.

sections.heading: 5.8 Semi-technical description of a typical flowering plant: floral formula and floral diagram
sections.body:
Various morphological features are used to describe a flowering plant. The description has to be brief, in simple and scientific language, and in a proper sequence. The plant is described beginning with its habit, then the vegetative characters (roots, stem and leaves) and then the floral characters (inflorescence and flower parts: calyx, corolla, androecium, gynoecium, fruit, seed). After describing the various parts, a floral diagram and a floral formula are presented. This sequence is itself a 2-mark answer ('what is a semi-technical description?').

Floral formula. The floral formula is represented by symbols. Br stands for bracteate, K for calyx, C for corolla, P for perianth, A for androecium, G for gynoecium, G with a line below it (written here as G̲) for a superior ovary and G with a line above it for an inferior ovary, ♂ for male, ♀ for female, ⚥ for bisexual, ⊕ for actinomorphic and % for zygomorphic. Fusion (cohesion, union of members of the same whorl) is indicated by enclosing the figure within a bracket, so K(5) means five united sepals and C5 means five free petals. Adhesion (union between different whorls, as epipetalous stamens) is shown by a line drawn above the symbols of the floral parts concerned, for example an arc joining C and A. A '+' inside a whorl shows members in two series, as A3+3 or A(9)+1.

Worked example (NCERT exercise 14): an actinomorphic, bisexual, hypogynous flower with five united sepals, five free petals, five free stamens and two united carpels with superior ovary and axile placentation is written ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C5 A5 G̲(2). Read it back: ⊕ actinomorphic, ⚥ bisexual, K(5) gamosepalous, C5 polypetalous, A5 five free stamens, G̲(2) two fused carpels with superior ovary (hypogynous). Axile placentation is not shown in the formula; it appears in the floral diagram.

Floral diagram. A floral diagram provides information about the number of parts of a flower, their arrangement and the relation they have with one another. The position of the mother axis with respect to the flower is represented by a dot on the top of the floral diagram. Calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium are drawn in successive whorls, calyx being the outermost and gynoecium in the centre. The floral diagram also shows cohesion and adhesion within parts of whorls and between whorls, and the transverse section of the ovary in the centre shows the number of locules and the placentation.

In an exam, the pair 'floral formula + floral diagram' is asked for Solanaceae almost every year. Write the formula in one line, draw the diagram with the dot on top, five sepals (united), five petals (united, valvate), five stamens attached to the petals, and a bilocular ovary with swollen axile placenta in the centre.

where: two carpels, united (syncarpous), ovary superior (line below G)

sections.tip: Brackets mean fusion within a whorl; a line drawn above two symbols means adhesion between whorls (epipetalous, epiphyllous). Superior ovary: line below G. Inferior ovary: line above G.

sections.heading: 5.9 Description of some important families: Solanaceae (with Fabaceae and Liliaceae as extension)
sections.body:
Solanaceae, the potato family (Solanum nigrum, potato, tomato, brinjal, chilli, petunia, tobacco). This is the one family retained in the rationalised NCERT print and it is asked for 3 or 5 marks with the floral formula and floral diagram.

Vegetative characters. Plants mostly herbs, shrubs, rarely small trees. Stem: herbaceous, rarely woody, aerial, erect, cylindrical, branched, solid or hollow, hairy or glabrous, underground stem in potato (tuber). Leaves: alternate, simple, rarely pinnately compound, exstipulate; venation reticulate.

Floral characters. Inflorescence: solitary, axillary or cymose as in Solanum. Flower: bisexual, actinomorphic. Calyx: sepals five, united (gamosepalous), persistent, valvate aestivation. Corolla: petals five, united (gamopetalous); valvate aestivation. Androecium: stamens five, epipetalous. Gynoecium: bicarpellary, syncarpous; ovary superior, bilocular, placenta swollen with many ovules, axile placentation. Fruit: berry (tomato, brinjal) or capsule (datura). Seeds: many, endospermous. Floral formula: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G̲(2), with a line of adhesion above C and A to show the epipetalous stamens.

Economic importance. Many plants of this family are a source of food (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicine (belladonna, ashwagandha), fumigatory (tobacco) and ornamentals (petunia).

Fabaceae (extension). The pea family, earlier called Papilionoideae, a subfamily of Leguminosae. Trees, shrubs, herbs; root with root nodules. Stem erect or climber. Leaves alternate, pinnately compound or simple; leaf base pulvinate; stipulate; reticulate venation. Inflorescence racemose. Flower bisexual, zygomorphic. Calyx: sepals five, gamosepalous; valvate or imbricate aestivation. Corolla: petals five, polypetalous, papilionaceous (a posterior standard, two lateral wings, two anterior ones forming a keel which encloses the stamens and pistil), vexillary aestivation. Androecium: ten stamens, diadelphous (9)+1, anthers dithecous. Gynoecium: ovary superior, monocarpellary, unilocular with many ovules, style single, marginal placentation. Fruit legume; seeds one to many, non-endospermic. Floral formula: % ⚥ K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G̲1. Economic importance: pulses (gram, arhar, sem, moong, soyabean), edible oil (soyabean, groundnut), dye (Indigofera), fibres (sunhemp), fodder (Sesbania, Trifolium), ornamentals (lupin, sweet pea), medicine (muliathi).

Liliaceae (extension). The lily family, a characteristic representative of monocotyledonous plants. Perennial herbs with underground bulbs, corms or rhizomes. Leaves mostly basal, alternate, linear, exstipulate with parallel venation. Inflorescence solitary or cymose, often umbellate clusters. Flower bisexual, actinomorphic. Perianth: tepals six (3+3), often united into a tube; valvate aestivation. Androecium: stamens six, (3+3), epiphyllous. Gynoecium: tricarpellary, syncarpous, ovary superior, trilocular with many ovules, axile placentation. Fruit capsule, rarely berry; seed endospermous. Floral formula: Br ⊕ ⚥ P(3+3) A3+3 G̲(3). Economic importance: ornamentals (tulip, Gloriosa), medicine (Aloe), vegetables (Asparagus), and the source of colchicine (Colchicum autumnale).

where: five stamens, epipetalous (line of adhesion between C and A)
bicarpellary, syncarpous, ovary superior, bilocular, axile placenta swollen
standard, two wings, two fused keel petals
six tepals in two whorls, united

sections.tip: For Solanaceae the marking scheme looks for: gamosepalous persistent calyx, gamopetalous corolla, valvate aestivation in both, five epipetalous stamens, bicarpellary syncarpous superior bilocular ovary with a swollen axile placenta, berry or capsule, endospermous seeds, and the formula. Tick them off one by one.

key_terms.definition: The study of the external form and structure of an organism; in this chapter, of the root, stem, leaf, inflorescence, flower, fruit and seed of a flowering plant.
The primary root formed by direct elongation of the radicle, together with its lateral roots of successive orders; typical of dicots such as mustard.
A cluster of thin roots arising from the base of the stem after the short-lived primary root dies; typical of monocots such as wheat.
Any root arising from a part of the plant other than the radicle, as in grass, Monstera and the banyan tree.
Very fine, delicate, thread-like unicellular extensions of epidermal cells in the region of maturation of the root; they absorb water and minerals from the soil.
Roots of swampy-area plants such as Rhizophora (mangrove) that grow vertically upward out of the soil and help the plant obtain oxygen for respiration.
The node is the region of the stem where leaves are borne; the internode is the portion of stem between two successive nodes.
A green, flattened (Opuntia) or fleshy cylindrical (Euphorbia) stem of arid-region plants that contains chlorophyll and photosynthesises in place of the leaves.
A flattened, green, expanded petiole that carries out photosynthesis in place of the small short-lived lamina, as in Australian Acacia.
The swollen leaf base found in some leguminous plants.
The arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina of a leaf; reticulate (network) in dicots, parallel in monocots.

A leaf whose lamina is incised right up to the midrib, breaking it into leaflets; pinnately compound when leaflets sit on a rachis (neem), palmately compound when they meet at the tip of the petiole (silk cotton).
The pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch: alternate (china rose, mustard, sunflower), opposite (Calotropis, guava) or whorled (Alstonia).

The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis; racemose when the main axis keeps growing and bears flowers laterally in acropetal succession, cymose when the main axis ends in a flower and flowers open in basipetal order.
The swollen end of the pedicel on which the four floral whorls, calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium, are arranged.
The outer whorls of a flower when calyx and corolla are not distinguishable, as in lily; its members are tepals.

A flower divisible into two equal halves by any radial plane through the centre is actinomorphic (mustard, datura, chilli); one divisible only in one vertical plane is zygomorphic (pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia).

Positions of the floral whorls relative to the ovary: gynoecium highest with a superior ovary (mustard, china rose, brinjal); other whorls on the rim of the thalamus at the same level, ovary half inferior (plum, rose, peach); thalamus fused around the ovary, ovary inferior (guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower).
The mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in a floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl: valvate, twisted, imbricate, vexillary.
Stamens attached to the petals are epipetalous (brinjal); stamens attached to the perianth are epiphyllous (lily).
Stamens united by their filaments into one bundle (china rose), two bundles (pea) or more than two bundles (citrus).
A gynoecium with free carpels is apocarpous (lotus, rose); one with fused carpels is syncarpous (mustard, tomato).
The arrangement of ovules within the ovary: marginal (pea), axile (china rose, tomato, lemon), parietal (mustard, Argemone), free central (Dianthus, Primrose), basal (sunflower, marigold).
A fruit formed from the ovary without fertilisation, hence seedless.
A one-seeded fleshy fruit developing from a monocarpellary superior ovary, with a thin epicarp, fleshy or fibrous mesocarp and stony endocarp, as in mango and coconut.
The proteinous outermost layer of the endosperm in a maize grain that separates the endosperm from the embryo.
The single large, shield-shaped cotyledon of a monocot (maize) embryo, lying against the endosperm.
The protective sheaths enclosing the plumule and the radicle respectively in a monocot embryo.

A symbolic one-line summary of a flower: Br bracteate, K calyx, C corolla, P perianth, A androecium, G gynoecium, line below G superior ovary, line above G inferior ovary, ⊕ actinomorphic, % zygomorphic, ⚥ bisexual; brackets show fusion, a line above symbols shows adhesion.

A drawing showing the number, arrangement and relation of floral parts as concentric whorls, with a dot on top marking the position of the mother axis and a transverse section of the ovary at the centre.

formula_sheet.name: Origin of root and shoot
formula_sheet.expr: Root system from the radicle; shoot system from the plumule of the embryo
formula_sheet.note: 1-mark favourite; tap root in dicots (mustard), fibrous in monocots (wheat), adventitious from non-radicle parts (grass, Monstera, banyan)

formula_sheet.name: Four regions of the root tip
formula_sheet.expr: Root cap → region of meristematic activity → region of elongation → region of maturation (root hairs)
formula_sheet.note: Meristematic cells small, thin-walled, dense protoplasm, divide repeatedly; elongation region gives growth in length; root hairs are unicellular epidermal extensions

formula_sheet.name: Functions of root and stem
formula_sheet.expr: Root: absorption of water and minerals, anchorage, storage of reserve food, synthesis of plant growth regulators. Stem: spreads branches with leaves, flowers, fruits; conducts water, minerals, photosynthates; storage, support, protection, vegetative propagation
formula_sheet.note: Give all four root functions; stem develops from plumule and bears nodes, internodes and buds

formula_sheet.name: Root modifications
formula_sheet.expr: Storage: carrot, turnip (tap), sweet potato (adventitious). Support: prop roots of banyan, stilt roots of maize and sugarcane. Respiration: pneumatophores of Rhizophora
formula_sheet.note: Extension section in the rationalised print, still asked in school papers and NEET

formula_sheet.name: Stem modifications
formula_sheet.expr: Storage/perennation: potato (tuber), ginger, turmeric (rhizome), zaminkand, Colocasia (corm). Climbing: tendrils from axillary buds in cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon, grapevine. Protection: thorns from axillary buds in Citrus, Bougainvillea. Photosynthesis: phylloclade of Opuntia (flattened), Euphorbia (fleshy cylindrical). Propagation: grass, strawberry (runner); mint, jasmine (stolon); Pistia, Eichhornia (offset); banana, pineapple, Chrysanthemum (sucker)
formula_sheet.note: Judge a stem by nodes, internodes, buds and scale leaves

formula_sheet.name: Leaf: parts and modifications
formula_sheet.expr: Leaf base (stipules; sheath in monocots; pulvinus in legumes), petiole, lamina with midrib. Modifications: tendril (pea), spine (cactus), fleshy storage leaves (onion, garlic), phyllode (Australian Acacia), insect traps (pitcher plant, venus fly trap)
formula_sheet.note: Leaves arise from the shoot apical meristem in acropetal order; bud in the axil of the petiole, never of a leaflet

formula_sheet.name: Venation, leaf types, phyllotaxy
formula_sheet.expr: Reticulate (dicots) / parallel (monocots). Simple / pinnately compound (neem, rachis) / palmately compound (silk cotton). Alternate (china rose, mustard, sunflower) / opposite (Calotropis, guava) / whorled (Alstonia)
formula_sheet.note: Each triplet is an MCQ set

formula_sheet.name: Inflorescence
formula_sheet.expr: Racemose: main axis grows on, flowers lateral, acropetal. Cymose: main axis ends in a flower, limited growth, basipetal
formula_sheet.note: Flower is a modified shoot: apical meristem → floral meristem, internodes do not elongate, floral appendages at successive nodes instead of leaves

formula_sheet.name: Flower symmetry and merosity
formula_sheet.expr: Actinomorphic: mustard, datura, chilli. Zygomorphic: pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia. Asymmetric: canna. Trimerous / tetramerous / pentamerous = parts in multiples of 3 / 4 / 5
formula_sheet.note: Bracteate = with bracts at the base of the pedicel; ebracteate = without

formula_sheet.name: Position of the ovary
formula_sheet.expr: Hypogynous, superior ovary: mustard, china rose, brinjal. Perigynous, half inferior: plum, rose, peach. Epigynous, inferior: guava, cucumber, ray florets of sunflower
formula_sheet.note: NCERT exercise 15; draw three thalamus sketches

formula_sheet.name: Aestivation
formula_sheet.expr: Valvate: Calotropis. Twisted: china rose, lady's finger, cotton. Imbricate: Cassia, gulmohur. Vexillary (papilionaceous): pea, bean, with standard, two wings, two keel petals
formula_sheet.note: Arrangement of sepals or petals in the bud relative to members of the same whorl

formula_sheet.name: Androecium terms
formula_sheet.expr: Anther bilobed, each lobe with two pollen sacs; staminode = sterile stamen; epipetalous (brinjal), epiphyllous (lily); polyandrous (free); monadelphous (china rose), diadelphous (pea), polyadelphous (citrus); unequal filaments in Salvia and mustard

formula_sheet.name: Gynoecium and placentation
formula_sheet.expr: Carpel = stigma + style + ovary; ovules on placenta; apocarpous (lotus, rose), syncarpous (mustard, tomato). Marginal: pea. Axile: china rose, tomato, lemon. Parietal (false septum): mustard, Argemone. Free central (no septa): Dianthus, Primrose. Basal (one ovule): sunflower, marigold
formula_sheet.note: Ovules → seeds, ovary → fruit after fertilisation

formula_sheet.name: Fruit
formula_sheet.expr: Mature ripened ovary; pericarp = epicarp + mesocarp + endocarp; parthenocarpic = without fertilisation, seedless; drupe (mango, coconut) from a monocarpellary superior ovary, one-seeded; mango edible part = mesocarp; coconut mesocarp fibrous
formula_sheet.note: True fruit from ovary alone; false fruit includes thalamus (apple)

formula_sheet.name: Dicot seed (gram, bean)
formula_sheet.expr: Seed coat: testa (outer) + tegmen (inner); hilum (scar of attachment), micropyle (pore above hilum); embryo = embryonal axis + two fleshy cotyledons; radicle and plumule at the two ends; endospermic (castor) or non-endospermic (bean, gram, pea)

formula_sheet.name: Monocot seed (maize)
formula_sheet.expr: Seed coat membranous, fused with the fruit wall; bulky endosperm; aleurone layer (proteinous) between endosperm and embryo; embryo in a groove with one shield-shaped cotyledon (scutellum), plumule in coleoptile, radicle in coleorhiza; monocot seeds generally endospermic, orchids non-endospermic
formula_sheet.note: the NCERT figure, the most asked diagram

formula_sheet.name: Floral formula symbols
formula_sheet.expr: Br bracteate; K calyx; C corolla; P perianth; A androecium; G gynoecium; line below G superior ovary; line above G inferior ovary; ♂ male; ♀ female; ⚥ bisexual; ⊕ actinomorphic; % zygomorphic; brackets = fusion; line above symbols = adhesion
formula_sheet.note: Exercise 14 answer: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C5 A5 G̲(2)

formula_sheet.name: Solanaceae
formula_sheet.expr: Herbs/shrubs; leaves alternate, simple, exstipulate, reticulate; inflorescence solitary, axillary or cymose; flower bisexual, actinomorphic; K(5) persistent valvate; C(5) valvate; A5 epipetalous; G̲(2) syncarpous, superior, bilocular, swollen axile placenta; fruit berry or capsule; seeds many, endospermous. ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G̲(2)
formula_sheet.note: Food: tomato, brinjal, potato; spice: chilli; medicine: belladonna, ashwagandha; fumigatory: tobacco; ornamental: petunia

diagrams.title: Parts of a flowering plant (NCERT Figure 5.1)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw one upright plant with the soil line across the middle. Below the line draw a tap root with lateral roots and label root system, primary root, lateral (secondary) root. Above the line draw a stem with three or four nodes, each bearing a leaf; mark node, internode, leaf, axillary bud in the angle between a leaf and the stem, and a terminal bud or flower at the tip. Add one flower with pedicel and one developing fruit, and label shoot system, stem, flower, fruit. Write 'root system from radicle, shoot system from plumule' beneath.

diagrams.title: Regions of the root tip (NCERT Figure 5.3)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a slightly tapering root tip about 8 cm tall. At the very bottom draw a thimble-shaped cap and label root cap. Just above it shade a short zone of tiny cells and label region of meristematic activity. Above that a longer zone of elongated cells labelled region of elongation. The top zone carries many fine lateral hairs drawn as thin lines from single epidermal cells; label region of maturation and root hairs. Add one lateral root emerging near the top if space allows. One-line function beside each region earns the extra mark.

diagrams.title: Leaf parts, pinnately and palmately compound leaves (NCERT figure)
diagrams.how_to_draw: First draw a simple dicot leaf: leaf base with two small stipules, a petiole, a lamina with a midrib and branching veins forming a network; label leaf base, stipule, petiole, lamina, midrib, vein, reticulate venation. Beside it draw a neem leaf: a rachis carrying paired leaflets, an axillary bud at the base of the petiole only; label rachis, leaflet, petiole, axillary bud, pinnately compound. Then a silk cotton leaf: five to seven leaflets radiating from one point at the tip of the petiole; label palmately compound. Show clearly that no bud sits in the axil of any leaflet.

diagrams.title: Racemose and cymose inflorescence (NCERT figure)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw two floral axes side by side. Racemose: a long main axis that continues upward, with flowers on short stalks along its sides, the largest open flowers at the bottom and smallest buds at the top; label main axis (unlimited growth), oldest flower at base, youngest at apex, acropetal. Cymose: a main axis that ends in a single large flower, with younger flowers arising below it on lateral branches; label terminal flower (oldest), main axis of limited growth, younger flowers below, basipetal.

diagrams.title: Position of floral parts on the thalamus: hypogynous, perigynous, epigynous (NCERT figure)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw three longitudinal sections of a flower. Hypogynous: a flat or convex thalamus with the ovary sitting on top and sepals, petals and stamens inserted below it; label superior ovary, example mustard or china rose. Perigynous: a cup-shaped thalamus with the ovary at the bottom of the cup and sepals, petals and stamens on the rim at about the level of the ovary; label half inferior ovary, example rose or plum. Epigynous: the thalamus cup fused completely round the ovary with sepals, petals and stamens arising above it; label inferior ovary, example guava or cucumber. In each, label thalamus, sepal, petal, stamen, ovary, style, stigma.

diagrams.title: Types of aestivation (NCERT figure)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw four small top-view rings of five petals each. Valvate: petals with edges just touching, no overlap; label Calotropis. Twisted: each petal overlapping the next one in the same direction all round, like a pinwheel; label china rose. Imbricate: petals overlapping without a regular direction, one petal fully outside, one fully inside, others one edge in and one out; label Cassia, gulmohur. Vexillary: one large posterior standard overlapping two lateral wings, which overlap two small anterior keel petals; label standard, wing, keel, pea. Write the definition of aestivation under the set.

diagrams.title: Types of placentation (NCERT figure)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw five transverse sections of an ovary as circles, and one longitudinal section for basal. Marginal: a single chamber with ovules in two rows along one side, the ventral suture; label pea. Axile: a circle divided into chambers by septa meeting at the centre, with ovules on the central axis; label china rose, tomato, lemon. Parietal: a single chamber with ovules on the inner wall, and optionally a false septum; label mustard, Argemone. Free central: a single chamber with a central column carrying ovules and no septa; label Dianthus, Primrose. Basal: a longitudinal section with one ovule at the base; label sunflower, marigold. Title the set 'placentation: arrangement of ovules within the ovary'.

diagrams.title: Structure of a dicot seed (gram or bean) and V.S. of a maize grain (NCERT figure)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Gram seed: draw the whole seed showing hilum and micropyle on the surface, then a split seed with the two large cotyledons and the small embryonal axis between them; label seed coat (testa outside, tegmen inside), hilum, micropyle, cotyledon, plumule, radicle, embryonal axis. Maize V.S.: draw an oblong grain in vertical section, with a large shaded endosperm occupying most of it, a thin outer layer labelled seed coat fused with fruit wall, a line just inside labelled aleurone layer, and the small embryo in a groove at one end: shield-shaped scutellum against the endosperm, plumule inside the coleoptile pointing up, radicle inside the coleorhiza pointing down. Eight labels are expected.

diagrams.title: Floral diagram and floral formula of Solanaceae (NCERT figure)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Put a dot at the top for the mother axis. Draw, from outside in: a ring of five united sepals with their edges touching (valvate), a ring of five united petals alternating with the sepals (valvate), five stamens drawn as small anther outlines lying opposite the sepals and joined to the petals to show they are epipetalous, and at the centre a transverse section of a bilocular ovary with two chambers and a swollen axile placenta bearing many ovules, the two carpels placed obliquely. Write the floral formula beneath: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G̲(2), with a line joining C and A to show adhesion.

ncert_questions.q: What is meant by modification of root? What type of modification of root is found in the (a) Banyan tree (b) Turnip (c) Mangrove trees?
ncert_questions.a:
Roots normally absorb water and minerals and anchor the plant. In some plants the root changes its shape and structure to perform a function other than absorption and conduction, such as support, storage of food or respiration. This change is called modification of root.

(a) Banyan tree: prop roots. Roots grow down from the horizontal branches, enter the soil and become thick pillar-like supports for the heavy spreading branches.

(b) Turnip: storage tap root. The tap root becomes swollen and fleshy and stores reserve food.

(c) Mangrove trees (Rhizophora): pneumatophores. In waterlogged, oxygen-poor swampy soil many roots grow vertically upwards out of the soil and help the plant get oxygen for respiration.

ncert_questions.q: Justify the following statements on the basis of external features: (i) Underground parts of a plant are not always roots. (ii) Flower is a modified shoot.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) A root is recognised by a root cap, root hairs and the absence of nodes, internodes, buds and leaves. Several underground parts fail this test and are therefore stems: the potato tuber has nodes and internodes, and its 'eyes' are axillary buds in the axils of scale leaves; ginger and turmeric rhizomes have nodes, internodes, scale leaves and buds; the onion bulb is a short conical stem carrying fleshy leaves and a terminal bud; zaminkand and Colocasia corms have nodes, scale leaves and buds. All of these are underground stems, so an underground part is not always a root.

(ii) A flower is a modified shoot because: the shoot apical meristem changes into a floral meristem; the internodes do not elongate, so the axis becomes condensed into the thalamus; the apex produces the floral appendages (sepals, petals, stamens, carpels) laterally at successive nodes, in the position where leaves would be produced; and when a shoot tip transforms into a flower it is always solitary. Sepals are often green and leaf-like, showing that they are modified leaves.

ncert_questions.q: How is a pinnately compound leaf different from a palmately compound leaf?
ncert_questions.a: In a compound leaf the incisions of the lamina reach the midrib and break it into leaflets. In a pinnately compound leaf a number of leaflets are borne on a common axis called the rachis, which represents the midrib of the leaf, as in neem. In a palmately compound leaf there is no rachis; the leaflets are attached at a common point, at the tip of the petiole, and spread out like the fingers of a palm, as in silk cotton (Bombax). In both, the bud is in the axil of the petiole and not in the axil of any leaflet.

ncert_questions.q: Explain with suitable examples the different types of phyllotaxy.
ncert_questions.a:
Phyllotaxy is the pattern of arrangement of leaves on the stem or branch. It is of three types.

Alternate: a single leaf arises at each node in an alternate manner, as in china rose, mustard and sunflower.

Opposite: a pair of leaves arises at each node, the two leaves lying opposite to each other, as in Calotropis and guava.

Whorled: more than two leaves arise at a node and form a whorl, as in Alstonia.

Phyllotaxy exposes the maximum leaf surface to light and reduces shading of one leaf by another.

ncert_questions.q: Define the following terms: (a) aestivation (b) placentation (c) actinomorphic (d) zygomorphic (e) superior ovary (f) perigynous flower (g) epipetalous stamen.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Aestivation: the mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in a floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl; valvate, twisted, imbricate or vexillary.

(b) Placentation: the arrangement of ovules within the ovary; marginal, axile, parietal, free central or basal.

(c) Actinomorphic: a flower that can be divided into two equal radial halves by any radial plane passing through the centre (radial symmetry), as in mustard, datura and chilli.

(d) Zygomorphic: a flower that can be divided into two similar halves only in one particular vertical plane (bilateral symmetry), as in pea, gulmohur, bean and Cassia.

(e) Superior ovary: the ovary of a hypogynous flower, where the gynoecium occupies the highest position on the thalamus and calyx, corolla and androecium are inserted below it, as in mustard, china rose and brinjal.

(f) Perigynous flower: a flower in which the gynoecium is in the centre of a cup-shaped thalamus and the other whorls are borne on the rim of the thalamus at almost the same level as the ovary; the ovary is half inferior, as in plum, rose and peach.

(g) Epipetalous stamen: a stamen whose filament is attached to (adnate to) a petal, as in brinjal and other members of Solanaceae.

ncert_questions.q: Differentiate between (a) Racemose and cymose inflorescence (b) Fibrous root and adventitious root (c) Apocarpous and syncarpous ovary.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Racemose: the main axis continues to grow (unlimited growth) and does not end in a flower; flowers are borne laterally in acropetal succession, the oldest at the base and youngest at the apex. Cymose: the main axis terminates in a flower (limited growth); flowers are borne in basipetal order, the terminal flower being the oldest and younger flowers arising below it.

(b) Fibrous root: a system of many thin roots of similar size arising from the base of the stem after the primary root dies, typical of monocots such as wheat. Adventitious root: any root arising from a part of the plant other than the radicle (from stem, branches or leaves), as in grass, Monstera and banyan; it may serve support, storage or propagation. Every fibrous root is adventitious in origin, but adventitious roots need not form a fibrous system.

(c) Apocarpous ovary: the gynoecium has more than one carpel and the carpels are free from one another, as in lotus and rose. Syncarpous ovary: the carpels are fused together, as in mustard and tomato.

ncert_questions.q: Draw the labelled diagram of the following: (i) gram seed (ii) V.S. of maize seed.
ncert_questions.a:
(i) Gram seed: draw the seed with the seed coat opened to show the two cotyledons. Labels: seed coat (testa outside, tegmen inside), hilum, micropyle, two cotyledons, embryonal axis, plumule, radicle. Non-endospermic; food stored in the fleshy cotyledons.

(ii) V.S. of maize grain: draw an oblong grain with a large endosperm and a small embryo in a groove at one end. Labels: seed coat fused with fruit wall, endosperm, aleurone layer, scutellum (single shield-shaped cotyledon), coleoptile enclosing the plumule, plumule, radicle, coleorhiza enclosing the radicle. Endospermic; food stored in the bulky endosperm.

(See the diagrams section for how to draw each so that it earns full marks.)

ncert_questions.q: Describe modifications of stem with suitable examples.
ncert_questions.a:
The stem is modified to perform functions other than bearing leaves and flowers.

Storage and perennation: underground stems of potato (tuber), ginger and turmeric (rhizome), zaminkand and Colocasia (corm) store food and help the plant survive unfavourable seasons.

Support (climbing): stem tendrils developing from axillary buds are slender and spirally coiled and help the plant climb, as in gourds (cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon) and grapevine.

Protection: axillary buds become woody, straight, pointed thorns that protect the plant from browsing animals, as in Citrus and Bougainvillea.

Photosynthesis: in arid-region plants the stem becomes flattened (Opuntia) or fleshy cylindrical (Euphorbia), contains chlorophyll and photosynthesises (phylloclade).

Vegetative propagation: underground stems of grass and strawberry spread to new niches and form new plants when the older parts die (runner); in mint and jasmine a slender lateral branch from the base of the main axis arches down to the ground (stolon); in Pistia and Eichhornia a lateral branch with short internodes bears a rosette of leaves and a tuft of roots at each node (offset); in banana, pineapple and Chrysanthemum lateral branches from the underground base grow horizontally under the soil and then come out obliquely to form leafy shoots (sucker).

ncert_questions.q: Take one flower of the family Solanaceae and write its semi-technical description. Also draw its floral diagram after studying it.
ncert_questions.a:
Solanum nigrum (family Solanaceae)

Habit: an annual herb.

Vegetative characters. Root: branched tap root. Stem: herbaceous, aerial, erect, cylindrical, branched, solid, glabrous or hairy. Leaves: alternate, simple, exstipulate, petiolate, reticulate venation.

Floral characters. Inflorescence: solitary, axillary or cymose. Flower: bisexual, actinomorphic, pentamerous, hypogynous. Calyx: sepals five, gamosepalous, persistent, valvate aestivation. Corolla: petals five, gamopetalous, rotate, valvate aestivation. Androecium: stamens five, epipetalous, alternating with the petals, anthers dithecous. Gynoecium: bicarpellary, syncarpous; ovary superior, bilocular, placenta swollen with many ovules, axile placentation; carpels placed obliquely; style one, stigma capitate. Fruit: berry. Seeds: many, endospermous.

Floral formula: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G̲(2), with a line of adhesion above C and A for the epipetalous stamens.

Floral diagram: dot at the top for the mother axis; five united sepals (outermost), five united petals alternating with them, five stamens attached to the petals, and at the centre a bilocular ovary with swollen axile placentae bearing many ovules.

Economic importance: food (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicine (belladonna, ashwagandha), fumigatory (tobacco), ornamentals (petunia).

ncert_questions.q: Describe the various types of placentations found in flowering plants.
ncert_questions.a:
Placentation is the arrangement of ovules within the ovary. It is of five types.

Marginal: the placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary and the ovules are borne on this ridge forming two rows, as in pea.

Axile: the placenta is axial and the ovules are attached to it in a multilocular ovary, as in china rose, tomato and lemon.

Parietal: the ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or on the peripheral part; the ovary is one-chambered but becomes two-chambered due to the formation of a false septum, as in mustard and Argemone.

Free central: the ovules are borne on the central axis and septa are absent, as in Dianthus and Primrose.

Basal: the placenta develops at the base of the ovary and a single ovule is attached to it, as in sunflower and marigold.

In the exam add a transverse-section sketch of each type with the ovules positioned correctly.

ncert_questions.q: What is a flower? Describe the parts of a typical angiosperm flower.
ncert_questions.a:
A flower is the reproductive unit of an angiosperm, meant for sexual reproduction; it is a modified shoot. A typical flower has four whorls arranged successively on the swollen end of the pedicel, the thalamus or receptacle.

Calyx: the outermost whorl of sepals, usually green and leaf-like, protecting the flower in the bud; gamosepalous (united) or polysepalous (free).

Corolla: the whorl of petals, usually brightly coloured to attract insects for pollination; gamopetalous or polypetalous; tubular, bell-shaped, funnel-shaped or wheel-shaped. Calyx and corolla are the accessory whorls; when they are not distinct (lily) they are called perianth.

Androecium: the whorl of stamens, the male reproductive organs. Each stamen has a filament and a bilobed anther, each lobe with two pollen sacs where pollen grains are produced. A sterile stamen is a staminode. Stamens may be epipetalous (brinjal) or epiphyllous (lily); free (polyandrous) or united into one (monadelphous, china rose), two (diadelphous, pea) or more bundles (polyadelphous, citrus).

Gynoecium: the female reproductive part, made of one or more carpels. Each carpel has a stigma (receptive surface for pollen), a style and an ovary containing ovules on a placenta. Carpels may be free (apocarpous: lotus, rose) or fused (syncarpous: mustard, tomato). After fertilisation the ovules become seeds and the ovary becomes the fruit.

Draw a labelled longitudinal section of a flower showing pedicel, thalamus, sepal, petal, stamen (filament, anther), carpel (stigma, style, ovary, ovule).

ncert_questions.q: How do the various leaf modifications help plants?
ncert_questions.a:
Leaves are modified to perform functions other than photosynthesis.

Tendrils: in pea the leaflets become thread-like coiling tendrils that help the weak-stemmed plant climb a support.

Spines: in cacti the leaves are reduced to spines that defend the plant against grazing animals and reduce water loss in the desert.

Storage: the fleshy leaves of onion and garlic store food.

Phyllode: in Australian Acacia the leaves are small and short-lived, and the petiole expands, turns green and synthesises food.

Insect trapping: in the pitcher plant and venus fly trap the leaves are modified to trap and digest insects, supplying nitrogen to plants growing in nitrogen-poor soil.

ncert_questions.q: Define the term inflorescence. Explain the basis for the different types of inflorescence in flowering plants.
ncert_questions.a:
The arrangement of flowers on the floral axis is termed the inflorescence.

The basis for the two major types is whether the apex of the floral axis gets converted into a flower or continues to grow. In a racemose inflorescence the main axis continues to grow and the flowers are borne laterally in acropetal succession (oldest at the base, youngest at the tip). In a cymose inflorescence the main axis terminates in a flower, so its growth is limited, and the flowers are borne in basipetal order (the terminal flower is the oldest, the younger ones arise below it).

ncert_questions.q: Write the floral formula of an actinomorphic, bisexual, hypogynous flower with five united sepals, five free petals, five free stamens and two united carpels with superior ovary and axile placentation.
ncert_questions.a:
⊕ ⚥ K(5) C5 A5 G̲(2)

⊕ actinomorphic; ⚥ bisexual; K(5) five united (gamosepalous) sepals; C5 five free (polypetalous) petals; A5 five free stamens; G̲(2) two united carpels (syncarpous) with the line below G showing the superior ovary of a hypogynous flower. The axile placentation is shown in the floral diagram as ovules on the central axis of a bilocular ovary; it does not appear in the formula.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the arrangement of floral members in relation to their insertion on thalamus.
ncert_questions.a:
Based on the position of calyx, corolla and androecium with respect to the ovary on the thalamus, flowers are of three kinds.

Hypogynous: the gynoecium occupies the highest position on the thalamus while the other parts are situated below it; the ovary is superior, as in mustard, china rose and brinjal.

Perigynous: the thalamus is cup-shaped; the gynoecium is situated in the centre and the other parts of the flower are located on the rim of the thalamus at almost the same level as the ovary; the ovary is said to be half inferior, as in plum, rose and peach.

Epigynous: the margin of the thalamus grows upward, enclosing the ovary completely and fusing with it, and the other parts of the flower arise above the ovary; the ovary is inferior, as in guava, cucumber and the ray florets of sunflower.

Draw three longitudinal sections showing the thalamus flat, cup-shaped, and fused round the ovary.

ncert_questions.q: Potato is a stem and sweet potato is a root. Justify on the basis of external features.
ncert_questions.a:
Potato is a stem: it has nodes and internodes; the eyes on its surface are axillary buds lying in the axils of small scale leaves; it develops at the tip of an underground branch (stolon) and can sprout new shoots from the eyes. It has no root cap and no root hairs.

Sweet potato is a root: it is a swollen adventitious root with no nodes, internodes, buds or scale leaves; it bears thin lateral rootlets along its length and its tip has a root cap. Both store food, but only the potato shows the external features of a stem.

pyq.q: Stilt roots are found in
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Maize and sugarcane have stilt roots from the lower nodes of the stem; banyan has prop roots, carrot a storage tap root and Rhizophora pneumatophores.

pyq.q: Which of the following has a pinnately compound leaf?
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Neem leaflets are borne on a rachis (pinnately compound); silk cotton is palmately compound; mustard and Calotropis have simple leaves.

pyq.q: Free central placentation is seen in
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Dianthus and Primrose have free central placentation; pea is marginal, mustard parietal and sunflower basal.

pyq.q: Valvate aestivation is found in
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: In Calotropis the petals just touch at the margins without overlapping (valvate). China rose is twisted, Cassia imbricate and pea vexillary.

pyq.q: An epigynous flower with an inferior ovary is found in
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Guava, cucumber and the ray florets of sunflower are epigynous. Mustard and brinjal are hypogynous; plum is perigynous.

pyq.q: In a maize grain, the proteinous layer that separates the embryo from the endosperm is the
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The aleurone layer is the outer proteinous covering of the endosperm; the scutellum is the cotyledon, the coleoptile the sheath of the plumule and the tegmen the inner seed coat of a dicot seed.

pyq.q: Whorled phyllotaxy is found in
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Alstonia bears more than two leaves at each node in a whorl. Guava is opposite; mustard and sunflower are alternate.

pyq.q: In the floral formula of Solanaceae, ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G̲(2), the brackets around 5 in K(5) indicate
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: A bracket encloses members of a whorl that are fused (cohesion), so K(5) means gamosepalous. Adhesion between whorls is shown by a line drawn above the symbols, not by brackets.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The potato tuber is a modified stem. Reason (R): The eyes of a potato are axillary buds present in the axils of scale leaves at the nodes.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Nodes, internodes, scale leaves and axillary buds are stem features; their presence is exactly why the potato is identified as a stem.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A bud is present in the axil of every leaflet of a compound leaf. Reason (R): The leaflets of a compound leaf are parts of a single leaf formed by incisions reaching the midrib.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: NCERT states that a bud is present in the axil of the petiole of both simple and compound leaves but not in the axil of the leaflets. So A is false; R correctly describes how a compound leaf forms.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Mango is a drupe. Reason (R): The edible part of mango is the stony endocarp.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Mango is a one-seeded drupe from a monocarpellary superior ovary, so A is true. The edible fleshy part is the mesocarp; the endocarp is the hard stone, so R is false.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): In a cymose inflorescence the flowers are borne in a basipetal order. Reason (R): In a cymose inflorescence the main axis terminates in a flower and so has limited growth.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Because the apex ends in the first (oldest) flower, later flowers must arise below it on lateral branches, giving the basipetal order. R explains A.

pyq.q: Define venation. Name its two types with one example each.
pyq.answer:
Venation is the arrangement of veins and veinlets in the lamina of a leaf. (1 mark)
