Reticulate venation: the veinlets form a network, as in dicotyledons (mustard, china rose, neem). Parallel venation: the veins run parallel to each other within the lamina, as in monocotyledons (wheat, maize, banana, grass). (1 mark)

pyq.q: Distinguish between prop roots and stilt roots with an example of each.
pyq.answer:
Prop roots arise from the horizontal aerial branches of the tree, hang down, enter the soil and become thick pillar-like supports for the spreading branches; example, banyan tree.

Stilt roots arise in clusters from the lower nodes of the stem and grow obliquely into the soil to support the stem; example, maize and sugarcane.

Both are adventitious roots modified for support.

pyq.q: What are pneumatophores? In which plant are they found and what is their function?
pyq.answer: Pneumatophores are roots of plants growing in swampy, waterlogged areas that come out of the soil and grow vertically upwards. They are found in Rhizophora, a mangrove plant. Since the swampy soil is poor in oxygen, these roots help the plant obtain oxygen for respiration through pores on their surface. They are a modification of roots for respiration.

pyq.q: Give two reasons to justify that the onion bulb is a modified stem.
pyq.answer: (i) The onion bulb has a short, condensed, conical stem (disc) at its base that bears nodes with fleshy scale leaves; the fleshy layers of the bulb are leaves, not root tissue. (ii) The stem bears a terminal bud (which sprouts into the green shoot) and axillary buds in the axils of the scale leaves, and adventitious roots arise from its base. Buds, nodes and leaves are stem characters; the bulb has no root cap or root hairs of its own.

pyq.q: Name the four regions of a root from the tip upward and state the function of root hairs.
pyq.answer:
From the tip upward: root cap, region of meristematic activity, region of elongation, region of maturation. (1 mark)

Root hairs are very fine, delicate, thread-like extensions of epidermal cells in the region of maturation; they absorb water and minerals from the soil and increase the absorbing surface of the root. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Differentiate between a phyllode and a phylloclade with an example of each.
pyq.answer:
A phyllode is a modified leaf: the petiole becomes flattened, green and leaf-like and carries out photosynthesis while the true lamina is small and short-lived, as in Australian Acacia.

A phylloclade is a modified stem: the stem becomes flattened (Opuntia) or fleshy cylindrical (Euphorbia), green and photosynthetic, while the leaves are reduced to spines. Both are adaptations of dry-region plants that reduce water loss.

pyq.q: Define aestivation. Name the type of aestivation found in china rose, Calotropis, Cassia and pea, and describe any two of them.
pyq.answer:
Aestivation is the mode of arrangement of sepals or petals in a floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl.

China rose: twisted. Calotropis: valvate. Cassia: imbricate. Pea: vexillary (papilionaceous).

Valvate: the sepals or petals in a whorl just touch one another at the margins without overlapping (Calotropis). Twisted: one margin of each appendage overlaps the margin of the next one, and so on all round in one direction (china rose, lady's finger, cotton). Imbricate: margins overlap one another but not in any particular direction (Cassia, gulmohur). Vexillary: of five petals, the largest posterior standard overlaps the two lateral wings, which in turn overlap the two smallest anterior keel petals (pea, bean).

pyq.q: Describe the structure of a monocot seed with the help of a labelled diagram of a vertical section of a maize grain, and give the function of the endosperm.
pyq.answer:
In maize the seed coat is membranous and generally fused with the fruit wall. The endosperm is bulky and stores food; its outer covering is a proteinous aleurone layer which separates the endosperm from the embryo. The embryo is small and lies in a groove at one end of the endosperm. It has one large shield-shaped cotyledon, the scutellum, and a short axis bearing the plumule (enclosed in the coleoptile) and the radicle (enclosed in the coleorhiza).

Function of endosperm: it is the food-storing tissue (mainly starch, with protein in the aleurone layer) that nourishes the embryo during germination; the scutellum absorbs the digested food and passes it to the growing embryo.

Diagram labels: seed coat fused with fruit wall, endosperm, aleurone layer, scutellum, coleoptile, plumule, radicle, coleorhiza.

pyq.q: Name the modification and state its function in each of the following: (i) Rhizophora (ii) Bougainvillea (iii) Pea.
pyq.answer:
(i) Rhizophora: pneumatophores, modified roots that grow vertically upward out of the swampy soil and obtain oxygen for respiration.

(ii) Bougainvillea: thorns, modified axillary buds of the stem that are woody, straight and pointed and protect the plant from browsing animals.

(iii) Pea: leaf tendrils, the terminal leaflets of the pinnately compound leaf modified into slender coiling structures that help the weak stem climb a support.

pyq.q: Differentiate between (i) actinomorphic and zygomorphic flowers, (ii) apocarpous and syncarpous ovary, (iii) racemose and cymose inflorescence. Give one example of each.
pyq.answer:
(i) An actinomorphic flower can be divided into two equal halves by any radial plane through the centre (mustard, datura, chilli); a zygomorphic flower can be divided into two similar halves only in one vertical plane (pea, gulmohur, bean, Cassia).

(ii) In an apocarpous gynoecium the carpels are free from one another (lotus, rose); in a syncarpous gynoecium the carpels are fused (mustard, tomato).

(iii) In a racemose inflorescence the main axis continues to grow and bears flowers laterally in acropetal succession (mustard); in a cymose inflorescence the main axis ends in a flower and the flowers are arranged in basipetal order (Solanum, jasmine).

pyq.q: Describe the different parts of a typical dicot leaf and mention the function of each.
pyq.answer: A typical leaf has three parts. Leaf base: attaches the leaf to the stem at the node; it may bear two small lateral stipules; in monocots it expands into a sheath that partly or wholly covers the stem, and in some legumes it is swollen into a pulvinus. Petiole: the stalk that holds the lamina up to the light; long, thin, flexible petioles let the blade flutter in the wind, cooling the leaf and bringing fresh air to its surface. Lamina (leaf blade): the green, expanded part with a prominent midrib and veins and veinlets; it is the seat of photosynthesis, and the veins give rigidity and act as channels for the transport of water, minerals and food.

pyq.q: Describe the various types of placentation found in flowering plants with the help of labelled diagrams.
pyq.answer:
Placentation is the arrangement of ovules within the ovary. The ovules are attached to a cushion-like tissue, the placenta, and its position defines five types.

1. Marginal: the placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary and the ovules are borne on this ridge in two rows; the ovary is monocarpellary and unilocular. Example: pea.

2. Axile: the carpels are fused and the placenta is on the central axis where the septa meet; the ovules are attached to this axis in a multilocular ovary. Examples: china rose, tomato, lemon.

3. Parietal: the ovules develop on the inner wall of the ovary or on its peripheral part; the ovary is one-chambered but becomes two-chambered by the formation of a false septum. Examples: mustard, Argemone.

4. Free central: the ovules are borne on a central axis and the septa are absent. Examples: Dianthus, Primrose.

5. Basal: the placenta develops at the base of the ovary and a single ovule is attached to it. Examples: sunflower, marigold.

Diagrams: five transverse sections of the ovary (basal in longitudinal section) showing the ovary wall, septa where present, the placenta and the ovules, each labelled with its type and example. (Definition 1 mark, five types with examples 2 marks, diagrams 2 marks.)

pyq.q: Write the semi-technical description of a plant of the family Solanaceae. Give its floral formula and draw its floral diagram. Mention two plants of economic importance from this family.
pyq.answer:
Solanaceae (Solanum nigrum)

Vegetative characters: plants mostly herbs, shrubs, rarely small trees. Stem herbaceous, rarely woody, aerial, erect, cylindrical, branched, solid or hollow, hairy or glabrous; underground stem in potato. Leaves alternate, simple, rarely pinnately compound, exstipulate; reticulate venation.

Floral characters: Inflorescence solitary, axillary or cymose as in Solanum. Flower bisexual, actinomorphic. Calyx: sepals five, united, persistent, valvate aestivation. Corolla: petals five, united, valvate aestivation. Androecium: stamens five, epipetalous. Gynoecium: bicarpellary, syncarpous; ovary superior, bilocular, placenta swollen with many ovules, axile placentation. Fruit: berry or capsule. Seeds: many, endospermous.

Floral formula: ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G̲(2), with a line above C and A showing the epipetalous condition.

Floral diagram: a dot at the top for the mother axis; outer whorl of five united sepals; five united petals alternating with the sepals; five stamens joined to the petals; central transverse section of a bilocular ovary with swollen axile placentae bearing many ovules, carpels obliquely placed.

Economic importance: food (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicine (belladonna, ashwagandha), fumigatory (tobacco), ornamental (petunia).

pyq.q: Describe the structure of a dicotyledonous seed and a monocotyledonous seed with labelled diagrams, and point out three differences between them.
pyq.answer:
Dicot seed (gram, bean): the outermost seed coat has two layers, the outer testa and the inner tegmen. The hilum is a scar on the seed coat through which the developing seed was attached to the fruit; above it is a small pore, the micropyle. Inside is the embryo: an embryonal axis and two fleshy cotyledons full of reserve food, with the radicle and plumule at the two ends of the axis. Castor seeds retain the endosperm (endospermic); bean, gram and pea consume it during development (non-endospermic).

Monocot seed (maize): the seed coat is membranous and fused with the fruit wall. The bulky endosperm stores food and is bounded by a proteinous aleurone layer that separates it from the embryo. The small embryo lies in a groove at one end and consists of a single shield-shaped cotyledon, the scutellum, and a short axis carrying the plumule enclosed in the coleoptile and the radicle enclosed in the coleorhiza. Monocot seeds are generally endospermic; orchid seeds are non-endospermic.

Differences: (i) two cotyledons versus one (scutellum); (ii) gram is non-endospermic with food in the cotyledons, maize is endospermic with food in the endosperm; (iii) the seed coat is distinct (testa and tegmen) in gram but membranous and fused with the fruit wall in maize; (iv) coleoptile and coleorhiza are present only in the monocot embryo.

Diagrams: gram seed with testa, tegmen, hilum, micropyle, cotyledons, plumule, radicle; V.S. of maize with seed coat fused to fruit wall, endosperm, aleurone layer, scutellum, coleoptile, plumule, radicle, coleorhiza.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A student dug up three underground parts from the kitchen garden: a potato, a piece of ginger and a sweet potato. The potato had several depressions with tiny buds inside them, the ginger was horizontal and bore rings and small papery scales, and the sweet potato was smooth and tapering with thin rootlets along its length.
(i) Which of the three are stems and which is a root? Give one external feature to support each identification.
(ii) Name the specific type of stem modification seen in the potato and in the ginger.
(iii) What are the depressions with buds on the potato called, and what is their morphological nature?
(iv) State two functions served by these underground modifications.
pyq.answer:
(i) Potato and ginger are stems; sweet potato is a root. The potato bears buds (eyes) at nodes, the ginger has nodes with scale leaves and internodes, both stem characters; the sweet potato has no nodes, buds or scale leaves and bears lateral rootlets, which is a root character.

(ii) Potato: tuber. Ginger: rhizome.

(iii) The depressions are the eyes of the potato; each eye is a node bearing an axillary bud (or a group of buds) in the axil of a small scale leaf.

(iv) Storage of food, and perennation, that is, surviving unfavourable conditions and giving rise to new plants (vegetative propagation) in the next growing season.

pyq.q:
Read the passage and answer the questions. A flower is described as follows: it is bracteate, bisexual, and can be cut into two equal halves along any radial plane. Its five sepals are green and fused into a cup that persists on the fruit; its five petals are fused; five stamens arise from the petals; the ovary is superior with two fused carpels, two chambers and many ovules on a swollen central placenta. The fruit is a fleshy berry.
(i) Write the floral formula of this flower.
(ii) Name the family and one plant of this family used as food.
(iii) What is the type of symmetry, the position of the ovary in relation to the thalamus, and the type of placentation?
(iv) What term describes the condition of the stamens, and how is it shown in the floral formula?
pyq.answer:
(i) Br ⊕ ⚥ K(5) C(5) A5 G̲(2)

(ii) Solanaceae; tomato, brinjal or potato (any one).

(iii) Actinomorphic (radial symmetry); the flower is hypogynous with a superior ovary; axile placentation on a swollen placenta in a bilocular ovary.

(iv) The stamens are epipetalous (adnate to the petals). Adhesion between whorls is shown in the floral formula by a line drawn above the symbols C and A.

practice_mcq.q: The root system of a flowering plant develops from the
practice_mcq.explanation: The radicle of the embryo elongates into the primary root; the plumule gives the shoot.
Some epidermal cells of the region of maturation extend into fine thread-like root hairs that absorb water and minerals.

practice_mcq.q: Adventitious roots are found in all of the following except
practice_mcq.explanation: Mustard has a tap root system from the radicle; grass, Monstera and banyan have adventitious roots arising from parts other than the radicle.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a swollen adventitious root?
practice_mcq.explanation: Carrot, turnip and radish are swollen tap roots; sweet potato is a swollen adventitious root.

practice_mcq.q: Stem tendrils of cucumber and grapevine develop from
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: stem tendrils which develop from axillary buds are slender and spirally coiled and help plants to climb, as in gourds and grapevines.

practice_mcq.q: The green, flattened, photosynthetic stem of Opuntia is called a
practice_mcq.explanation: A phylloclade is a flattened (Opuntia) or fleshy cylindrical (Euphorbia) green stem; a phyllode is a flattened petiole (Australian Acacia).

practice_mcq.q: A swollen leaf base found in some leguminous plants is called
practice_mcq.explanation: The pulvinus is the swollen leaf base of legumes; a sheath is the expanded leaf base of monocots; stipules are lateral outgrowths of the leaf base; the rachis is the axis of a pinnately compound leaf.
Guava and Calotropis have a pair of leaves at each node (opposite); china rose and mustard are alternate; Alstonia is whorled.

practice_mcq.q: In a racemose inflorescence the flowers are arranged in
options: Basipetal order with the main axis ending in a flower
Acropetal order with the main axis continuing to grow
Acropetal order with the main axis ending in a flower
Basipetal order with the main axis continuing to grow
practice_mcq.explanation: Racemose: unlimited growth of the main axis, flowers lateral, oldest at the base and youngest at the tip (acropetal).

practice_mcq.q: An asymmetric flower is found in
practice_mcq.explanation: Canna cannot be divided into two similar halves by any vertical plane. Datura and chilli are actinomorphic, Cassia is zygomorphic.

practice_mcq.q: Perigynous flowers with a half inferior ovary are found in
practice_mcq.explanation: In plum, rose and peach the floral whorls sit on the rim of a cup-shaped thalamus at the level of the ovary. Mustard, brinjal, china rose are hypogynous; guava and cucumber are epigynous.
China rose stamens are united into one bundle (monadelphous); pea is diadelphous, citrus polyadelphous, lily epiphyllous.

practice_mcq.q: Parietal placentation with a false septum is characteristic of
practice_mcq.explanation: In mustard and Argemone the ovules are on the inner wall of a one-chambered ovary that becomes two-chambered by a false septum. Pea is marginal, tomato axile, marigold basal.

practice_mcq.q: A fruit formed without fertilisation of the ovary is called
practice_mcq.explanation: Parthenocarpic fruits develop from an unfertilised ovary and are seedless, as in banana.

practice_mcq.q: The edible part of coconut is the
practice_mcq.explanation: In coconut the mesocarp is fibrous (coir) and the endocarp is the hard shell; the white edible flesh and the water are the endosperm of the seed.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following seeds is non-endospermic?
practice_mcq.explanation: In bean, gram and pea the endosperm is consumed by the developing embryo, so mature seeds lack it. Castor, maize and wheat are endospermic.

practice_mcq.q: The single shield-shaped cotyledon of the maize embryo is the
practice_mcq.explanation: The scutellum is the cotyledon; the coleoptile and coleorhiza are the sheaths of plumule and radicle; the aleurone layer is the proteinous outer layer of the endosperm.

practice_mcq.q: In a floral formula, adhesion between the corolla and androecium (epipetalous stamens) is shown by
options: A plus sign between C and A
A line drawn above the symbols C and A
practice_mcq.explanation: Brackets show fusion within a whorl (cohesion); a line drawn above the symbols shows adhesion between whorls.

common_mistakes: Writing 'potato is a root because it grows underground'. The examiner wants external stem features: nodes, internodes, eyes as axillary buds in the axils of scale leaves. Likewise sweet potato is a root (no nodes, no buds, has rootlets).

Mixing up stem tendrils and leaf tendrils, and thorns and spines. Cucumber, pumpkin, watermelon and grapevine have stem tendrils from axillary buds; pea has leaf tendrils. Citrus and Bougainvillea have thorns (stem); Opuntia and other cacti have spines (leaf).
Confusing phyllode with phylloclade. Phyllode is a flattened petiole (Australian Acacia); phylloclade is a flattened or fleshy stem (Opuntia, Euphorbia). Marks are lost for swapping the examples.

Marking a bud in the axil of every leaflet when drawing a compound leaf. NCERT is explicit: a bud is present in the axil of the petiole but not in the axil of the leaflets. This is also a favourite Assertion–Reason trap.

Defining aestivation without the phrase 'in the floral bud with respect to the other members of the same whorl', and describing twisted and imbricate as the same thing. Twisted overlaps in one direction; imbricate overlaps in no particular direction.

Confusing axile and free central placentation. Both have ovules on a central column; axile has septa dividing the ovary into chambers (china rose, tomato, lemon), free central has no septa (Dianthus, Primrose).

Reversing the ovary positions: hypogynous means superior ovary, epigynous means inferior ovary, perigynous means half inferior. Students write 'hypogynous, inferior' because 'hypo' sounds like below; remember the other whorls are below the ovary, so the ovary is on top.

Writing the floral formula with the wrong brackets and lines. Brackets enclose united members of the same whorl (K(5)); a line above two symbols shows adhesion between whorls (epipetalous); the line below G means superior ovary. Leaving out the ⊕ and ⚥ symbols also costs a mark.

Labelling the maize grain diagram with dicot terms (testa, tegmen, two cotyledons). The maize seed coat is membranous and fused with the fruit wall; there is one cotyledon (scutellum), an aleurone layer, a coleoptile and a coleorhiza.

Calling coconut water or flesh the mesocarp. In coconut the mesocarp is the fibrous coir, the endocarp is the shell, and the edible part is the endosperm of the seed. In mango the edible pulp is the mesocarp.
strategy:
This chapter is learned by table, diagram and example, not by long reading. Spend the first sitting making three tables and then revise only the tables. Table one: modifications, with columns for organ (root, stem, leaf), name of modification, function and NCERT example; there are about twenty rows and every MCQ on modifications is one row of this table. Table two: the flower vocabulary, with the term, its definition in one line and the NCERT example: symmetry (three), ovary position (three), aestivation (four), stamen conditions (epipetalous, epiphyllous, monadelphous, diadelphous, polyadelphous), carpel fusion (two) and placentation (five). Table three: the semi-technical description of Solanaceae written as a list of headings, from habit to seeds, with the floral formula at the bottom.

Diagrams are the second sitting. Draw, from memory and against the clock, the regions of the root, the three ovary positions, the four aestivations, the five placentations, the gram seed and the V.S. of maize, and the floral diagram of Solanaceae. Each should take under three minutes and carry every NCERT label. A neat labelled diagram alone often earns half the marks of a 3-mark or 5-mark question, so this is the best return on time in the whole paper.

Third sitting: write out the NCERT exercise answers in full, especially exercises 2, 5, 6, 10, 11, 14 and 15, because school papers lift them almost unchanged. Then practise the two justification questions ('underground parts are not always roots', 'flower is a modified shoot') until the four-point argument comes automatically.

In the exam, answer definition questions with the NCERT sentence plus an example, list questions as numbered points with one example each, and never leave a diagram question without the diagram. Allocate about a minute per mark, and draw before you write on the long questions so that the figure is never dropped for lack of time.
